A.explanation: Too small by a factor of 10, from an error in powers of 10 when converting $100 \text{ MW}$ and the input power in $\text{W}$.

B.explanation: Less than 50% and does not match $100 \text{ MW}$ divided by the gravitational input power of about $177 \text{ MW}$.

C.explanation: Matches $100 \text{ MW}$ divided by the input power $(1.5 \times 10^5 \times 9.81 \times 120) \text{ W}$, about 57%.

D.explanation: Too large, from underestimating the gravitational input power, for example by using $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ incorrectly combined with rounding.

hints: Notice the question gives mass flowing per unit time $1.5 \times 10^5 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$, not a single mass, and a fall height of $120 \text{ m}$.
The input is gravitational potential energy lost per second, so input power is $(m/t)gh$ with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Calculate the input power in $\text{MW}$, then form $\text{efficiency} = 100 \text{ MW}$ divided by that input power.
walkthrough: Identify the energy input per second: water of mass $m$ loses $mgh$ falling through $h = 120 \text{ m}$, while the useful output power is $P_{out} = 100 \text{ MW} = 100 \times 10^6 \text{ W}$.
State the rule: $\text{efficiency} = P_{useful\;output} / P_{total\;input}$, and $P_{input} = \text{energy supplied per second} = (m/t)gh$.
Substitute with units: $P_{input} = (1.5 \times 10^5 \text{ kg s}^{-1})(9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2})(120 \text{ m})$.
Form the ratio: $\text{efficiency} = (100 \times 10^6)/(177 \times 10^6) \approx 0.565$, or about 57% after multiplying by 100%. This is option C.
